title: Let's integrate AI Agents in Event-Sourced Systems — Divakar Kumar, FlyersSoft

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's central focus is structuring AI agents in a multi-agent system: a fan-out pattern dispatching gray-zone events to parallel agents (risk analyzer + behavior analyzer), whose outputs feed a third verdict agent. Agent loops with safeguard metrics to prevent infinite iteration, agent components (language model, tools, memory), and the control plane coordinating these agents via saga-style orchestration are all core topics. This matches the inclusion criteria for agent loops, planning, multi-agent design, and harness architecture.

secondary.label: Orchestration & Durable Execution
secondary.rationale: The talk describes a saga orchestration pattern where verdicts are emitted as events back to a message broker, continuing through payment and transaction bounded contexts. The orchestrator layer coordinates async communication across bounded contexts. However, the focus is on the agent architecture sitting atop this orchestration rather than on durability, retries, or checkpointing per se.

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: The semantic/materialized view layer aggregates data from all bounded contexts (transaction, device, account, payment) into a unified context that agents read to reason over the full domain. Short-term in-memory memory is used to meet sub-500ms SLA, with long-term memory explicitly excluded. This is context construction for agent reasoning, though not classic context-window management.

secondary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations
secondary.rationale: Agents are described as having tools for accessing external APIs and projection-layer data: fraud histories, device trust scores, migrated business rules, and behavior pattern plugins. Tool access is a component of the agent architecture but is not the primary focus of the talk.

domains.label: Finance & Trading
domains.rationale: The entire system is a payments and fraud detection platform. Transactions, chargebacks, KYC status, and device trust scoring are all financial services and risk concepts matching the 'Financial services, risk, and trading systems' domain description.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The system is deployed as enterprise infrastructure for real-time transaction processing and fraud detection workflows. The tiered architecture with rule-based, ML, and agentic layers represent an enterprise operational system, though the primary domain is financial services.

summary: Divakar Kumar presents a case study on integrating AI agents into an existing event-sourced payments and fraud detection system at FlyersSoft. The core problem is the "gray zone"—transactions that neither rule-based engines nor ML models can confidently classify. Rather than replacing existing systems, his team adds a Tier 2 agentic AI layer atop Tier 1 (rules + ML). The architecture leverages DDD bounded contexts (transaction, account, device, payment) that do not share data directly, coordinated asynchronously via saga orchestration through a message broker. Event sourcing with Cosmos DB stores domain events as immutable business facts; change data capture (change feeds) propagates these events to read models and a materialized semantic view that agents read for contextual reasoning. In the Tier 2 agentic layer, a fan-out pattern dispatches each gray-zone event to two parallel agents—a risk analyzer (tools for fraud histories, device trust, migrated business rules) and a behavior analyzer (transaction pattern plugins)—whose outputs feed a third verdict agent that synthesizes conclusions. This third-agent approach replaced an earlier metrics-based verdict that reproduced rule-based limitations and caused false positives. The verdict is emitted as an event back to the message broker, continuing the saga flow through payment and transaction contexts. Agent architecture comprises a language model (potentially an SLM or open-source model), tools for external API and projection access, and short-term in-memory memory to meet a sub-500ms SLA, with safeguard metrics to prevent infinite processing loops. A POC with synthetic data demonstrates the full architecture end-to-end on serverless infrastructure.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts are tightly coupled in this architecture: event sourcing provides the immutable event history that serves as natural agent memory, while CDC/change feeds and projection layers build a materialized semantic view that gives agents cross-context reasoning capability without violating DDD bounded context boundaries. The saga orchestration pattern provides the control plane through which agent verdicts flow back into business workflows. The fan-out multi-agent pattern and verdict agent synthesis represent the AI control logic layered on top of these event-driven infrastructure patterns. Without the event-sourced foundation, agents would lack the contextual history they need; without the agent layer, the event-sourced system cannot resolve gray-zone cases. The tiered architecture explicitly bridges these: existing SE infrastructure (event store, CDC, projections, saga) provides the substrate, while the AI agent patterns (fan-out, verdict synthesis, safeguard loops) consume that substrate to handle ambiguous cases the deterministic systems cannot. This matters as a blueprint for enterprises that want to add agentic AI without replacing proven event-driven architectures.
temporalContext: The video was published on 2026-07-30 on the AI Engineer YouTube channel, presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. The speaker also presented variants of this talk at DDD Europe 2026 (Antwerp) and FABCON 2026 (Atlanta, March 18). The talk describes existing infrastructure (rule-based engine ~5 years old, third-party ML model added later) and a POC with synthetic data. Research was conducted as of 2026-08-23. The discussion reflects the state of agentic AI integration in financial systems as of mid-2026, when enterprise adoption of multi-agent patterns atop event-driven architectures was an active frontier.
takeaways: Agents should be layered on top of existing rule-based and ML systems, handling only ambiguous gray-zone cases, not replacing Tier 1

concepts.name: Multi-Agent Fan-Out Pattern
concepts.explanation: Each gray-zone event is dispatched to two parallel agents—a risk analyzer and a behavior analyzer—that independently analyze the transaction before their outputs are synthesized by a verdict agent.
concepts.importance: This is the core agent architecture pattern in the talk, demonstrating how parallel independent analysis improves verdict quality over single-agent or rule-based approaches.

concepts.name: Verdict Agent Synthesis
concepts.explanation: A third agent analyzes the responses of the two parallel analysis agents and renders a final verdict, which is emitted as an event back to the message broker. This replaced a metrics-based verdict that reproduced rule-based limitations and caused false positives.
concepts.importance: Shows the evolutionary improvement from hard-coded verdicts to agent-synthesized verdicts, a key design lesson for multi-agent systems.

concepts.name: Gray-Zone Tiered AI Architecture
concepts.explanation: Tier 1 (rule-based engine + ML model) handles clear-cut approve/block cases, while Tier 2 (agentic AI) handles only ambiguous gray-zone transactions. The agentic layer is additive, not a replacement.
concepts.importance: Defines the architectural strategy of layering agents for only the cases where deterministic systems fail, a practical pattern for enterprise adoption.

concepts.name: Agent Loop Safeguard Metrics
concepts.explanation: Agent processing loops continue using tools until an end goal is reached, but teams must define metrics-based thresholds to break out and avoid infinite iteration, with thresholds varying by use case.
concepts.importance: Addresses a critical production concern: unbounded agent loops. The safeguard metric pattern is essential for deploying agents in real-time, SLA-constrained systems.

concepts.name: Agent Context via Semantic Layer
concepts.explanation: Agents gather context from projection layers via the semantic materialized view rather than querying bounded contexts directly. The semantic layer aggregates denormalized data across transaction, device, account, and payment contexts.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how to provide agents with cross-domain context without violating DDD bounded context boundaries or incurring multi-service query latency.

concepts.name: Event Sourcing
concepts.explanation: Domain events are stored as immutable business facts appended to an event store (Cosmos DB) rather than mutating current state. This provides a complete audit trail and natural memory layer that agents can replay.
concepts.importance: Foundational to the talk: event sourcing carries all the state and history that agents need to reason over, eliminating the need for a separate agent memory store.

concepts.name: Saga Orchestration
concepts.explanation: A saga orchestration pattern coordinates asynchronous communication across bounded contexts via a message broker. Verdict events are emitted back to the broker, continuing the flow through payment and transaction contexts.
concepts.importance: Provides the control plane that lets agent verdicts propagate through downstream bounded contexts without tight coupling.

concepts.name: Bounded Contexts (DDD)
concepts.explanation: The domain is organized into bounded contexts—transaction, account, device, and payment—each with its own data and logic. Contexts do not share data directly, requiring asynchronous communication patterns.
concepts.importance: Defines the domain boundaries that the semantic layer must aggregate across and that agents must respect when gathering context.

concepts.name: Change Data Capture (CDC) / Change Feed
concepts.explanation: Cosmos DB change feeds notify on data changes, propagating domain events to read models and worker processes that build projection layers. This is the propagation mechanism between event store and semantic layer.
concepts.importance: Bridges the gap between event store and agent-readable projections without direct database coupling.

concepts.name: Materialized View / Semantic Layer
concepts.explanation: A worker process (projection layer) aggregates denormalized data from all bounded contexts into a materialized view that provides a unified semantic context for agent reasoning.
concepts.importance: This is the key integration artifact that makes cross-context data available to agents as a single coherent context.

concepts.name: Read Models / Projections
concepts.explanation: Projection layers contain denormalized transaction counts and averages, device trust scores and location histories, account KYC status and age, and recent payment data—built from domain events.
concepts.importance: These projections are the concrete data structures that feed agent tools, enabling granular context lookups without querying the event store directly.

sections.title: Introduction: adding agents to an existing system
sections.summary: Divakar introduces the session goal: learning to integrate AI agents into existing business systems—not just chatbots or coding assistants, but real business workflows. The problem space is real-time fraud detection.

sections.title: A declined transaction you can't explain
sections.summary: Personal anecdote of a $3,500 laptop purchase being declined twice. Customer service called to verify but couldn't explain why the transaction was blocked—neither they nor the system provided an explanation. This uncertainty is the target area for AI agents.

sections.title: Where rule-based and ML systems fall short
sections.summary: Rule-based engine existed 5 years prior but was hard to maintain as fraudsters adapted. An ML model was added with a third-party provider. Both handle clear cases but leave gray-zone transactions unresolved. The approach: Tier 1 (rules + ML) handles most cases; Tier 2 (agentic AI) handles the gray zone.

sections.title: Bounded contexts: transaction, device, account, payment
sections.summary: The domain uses DDD bounded contexts: transaction (merchant, amount), account (KYC, customer info), device (fingerprints, OS), and payment (chargebacks). These contexts don't share data directly. An orchestrator layer (saga-style) with agentic AI coordinates communication asynchronously through a message broker.

sections.title: Event sourcing and change feeds
sections.summary: Transaction context emits domain events and receives integration events. Events are stored in Cosmos DB using event sourcing—appending as business facts without mutating state. Change feeds (CDC) notify on changes, propagating to read models. Events also go to a message broker for async processing by other teams.

sections.title: Building the semantic layer
sections.summary: All bounded contexts propagate events via CDC or message broker to a worker process (projection layer), which stores data in a materialized view (semantic layer). This unified view is what agents read to reason over the full domain context.

sections.title: Agent components and memory
sections.summary: Agents comprise a language model (can be SLM or open-source), tools for external API interaction, and a memory layer. Short-term in-memory memory meets the sub-500ms SLA. The agent decomposes queries into sub-tasks using reasoning, processing with tools until the end goal is reached.

sections.title: Avoiding infinite loops
sections.summary: The agent loop continues processing with tools until the end goal is reached. Teams must define metrics-based thresholds to break out of the loop, as these thresholds vary by use case. Avoiding infinite loops is a critical design consideration.

sections.title: Tier separation and fan-out pattern
sections.summary: The orchestration layer is segregated into Tier 1 (rule-based and ML engines) and Tier 2 (agentic AI). The Tier 2 layer uses a fan-out pattern: each gray-zone event is dispatched to two parallel agents—a risk analyzer agent and a behavior analyzer agent.

sections.title: Verdict agent and saga flow
sections.summary: Initially the verdict was metrics-based (an if-condition or metric), but this reproduced rule-based limitations and caused false positives. A third verdict agent now analyzes both agents' responses and renders a conclusion, emitted as an event back to the message broker. The saga flow continues through payment context (approving payments) and back to transaction context.

sections.title: Agent tools and context gathering
sections.summary: The risk analyzer agent has tools for fraud histories, device trust, and migrated business rules. The behavior analyzer agent analyzes transaction patterns via plugins. Agents gather context from projection layers: transaction (denormalized counts, averages, recent transactions), device (trust scores, location histories, IP addresses), account (KYC status, account age), and payment (recent payments).

sections.title: Putting the architecture together and POC demo
sections.summary: The high-level architecture works with any event source (relational or NoSQL database); the semantic layer provides context to AI agents. The agentic layer includes the verdict tool and short-term memory. A POC with synthetic data demonstrates events propagating through contexts, two agents producing conclusions, and a third verdict agent rendering the final decision on serverless infrastructure.

technologies.label: Fan-Out/Fan-In Multi-Agent Orchestration
technologies.summary: The fan-out/fan-in pattern is the central multi-agent architecture in the talk: each gray-zone transaction event is dispatched to two parallel agents—a risk analyzer (with tools for fraud histories, device trust, and migrated business rules) and a behavior analyzer (with transaction pattern plugins)—whose outputs feed a third verdict agent that synthesizes conclusions. This third-agent approach replaced an earlier metrics-based verdict that reproduced rule-based limitations and caused false positives. Agent processing loops continue with tools until an end goal is reached, with safeguard metrics to break out and avoid infinite iteration. The speaker's GitHub repository (Cloud-Jas/DurableMultiAgents) implements the same fan-out/fan-in pattern using Azure Durable Functions and Semantic Kernel, verified via Microsoft's On .NET Live show and the Azure Cosmos DB gallery.
technologies.role: Core architectural pattern defining how agents are structured to handle ambiguous gray-zone transactions—the central problem addressed in the talk. The fan-out dispatch to parallel agents and verdict synthesis by a third agent is the primary technical contribution.

technologies.label: Event Sourcing as Agent Memory Layer
technologies.summary: Event sourcing stores domain events as immutable business facts in Cosmos DB, providing the complete state and history that agents need to reason over the domain. When a user initiates a command, it goes into the event store as a business fact without mutating current state. Change feeds (CDC) notify on changes and propagate events to read models. The speaker explicitly states that event sourcing already carries the state and history agents need, making it a natural foundation for agentic AI and eliminating the need for a separate agent memory store. Long-term memory is excluded due to sub-500ms SLA constraints, with only short-term in-memory memory used in the agent architecture.
technologies.role: Foundational infrastructure providing the immutable event history that serves as the agent memory layer. Without event sourcing, agents would lack the historical context to reason over transaction patterns, device trust evolution, and account behavior over time.

technologies.label: Saga Orchestration for Agent Workflows
technologies.summary: Saga orchestration coordinates asynchronous communication across DDD bounded contexts (transaction, account, device, payment) via a message broker. The orchestrator dispatches gray-zone events to the Tier 2 agentic layer, and the verdict emitted by the verdict agent flows back through the message broker into payment context (approving/rejecting payments) and back to transaction context, continuing the saga flow. This pattern lets agent verdicts propagate through downstream business workflows without tight coupling between bounded contexts, which cannot share data directly.
technologies.role: Control plane that carries agent verdicts through downstream payment and transaction bounded contexts, completing the end-to-end flow from gray-zone detection to payment resolution. This is what makes agent outputs actionable in the real business system.

technologies.label: Semantic Layer / Materialized View for Agent Context
technologies.summary: The semantic layer (materialized view) aggregates denormalized data from all bounded contexts—transaction counts and averages, device trust scores and location histories, account KYC status and age, recent payment data—into a unified read model that agents query for contextual reasoning. A worker process (projection layer) builds this view from events propagated via CDC or message broker. The speaker explicitly describes how each bounded context denormalizes its data into the semantic layer: the transaction context contributes counts, averages, and recent transactions; the device context contributes trust scores and locations; the account context contributes KYC status and age; the payment context contributes recent payment data. This pattern enables agents to access cross-domain context without directly querying bounded contexts, respecting DDD boundaries while providing a single coherent context for agent reasoning.
technologies.role: Key integration artifact that makes cross-context data available to agents as a single coherent context. Agents read the semantic layer rather than querying bounded contexts directly, enabling cross-domain reasoning without violating DDD boundaries or incurring multi-service query latency under the sub-500ms SLA.
